comments.body:
Additional validation from RTX 5090 / Blackwell (PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, Triton 3.7.1), using the issue's attached guard-region repro:

- `R0_BLOCK=128`: 10/10 trials changed exactly **16,384** guard `uint64` words. Each trial produced **434,368–608,064 NaN / incorrect output elements**.
- `R0_BLOCK=256`: 10/10 trials preserved the guard (**0 changed words**) with **0 NaNs / 0 incorrect elements**.

I also rechecked the current `main` source (today's main moved while testing): the split-scan heuristic still clamps only the initial configs, so a `CoordescTuner` built from that metadata can generate the 128 neighbour; the autotune-cache load path also accepts a cached 128 dynamic/coordesc config. A local source-overlay candidate that propagates the existing split-scan lower bound into the generic `min_rblock` legality constraint removes the 128 neighbour, and applying the same lower-bound check when reconstructing cached dynamic configs rejects the stale 128 cache entry.

I am still **not opening a PR while the issue is in `triage review`**, per the contribution policy. Happy to submit the tested patch once maintainers mark it actionable.

issue.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Background: I modernized the Informer2020 repo and, with Codex's help, made
it torch.compile-compatible and CUDA graph tree compatible under
mode="max-autotune", running on my training workstation (NVIDIA H100 80GB
HBM3, accessed via SSH). During that work I noticed
intermittent nondeterminism (NaNs / corrupted tensors) that didn't correlate
with anything in the model logic itself.

GPT Astra Medium produced the following analysis of a plausible root cause:

> In `torch==2.13.0+cu132`, split-scan workspace sizing assumes
> `R0_BLOCK >= triton.min_split_scan_rblock` (256 by default). The initial
> heuristic configurations honor this, but coordinate-descent tuning can
> select 128, and the autotune cache accepts that configuration. The smaller
> block launches more scan programs, which read/write beyond the generated
> workspace.
>
> Workspace allocated: `8192 * ceil(576 / 256) * 8 = 196608` bytes.
> Workspace required: `8192 * ceil(576 / 128) * 8 = 327680` bytes.
> Overrun: **131072 bytes**.

I have not personally verified the specific internal function names in that
analysis (e.g. exact methods in coordinate_descent_tuner.py / autotune_cache.py),
so I'm not asserting those as fact — I'm including it as context for why this
workspace-sizing scheme is unsafe, not as a confirmed code path.

What I have verified myself, directly, with a standalone repro
(`workspace_repro.py`, attached) that exercises a split-scan-style kernel with
a guard region packed with a NaN/ready-flag sentinel — independent of any
model, dataset, or CUDA graphs — on two separate machines:

**H100 (SSH training workstation):**
- `--block-size 128`: guard region corrupted on 10/10 trials — 16384 guard
  words changed every trial, 551,168-695,936 NaN outputs per trial.
- `--block-size 256`, same workspace allocation (196608 bytes): clean on
  10/10 trials — 0 guard words changed, 0 NaNs, exact output.

**RTX 4050 Laptop GPU (local machine):**
- `--block-size 128`: guard region corrupted on 10/10 trials, reproduced
  across two separate runs — 16384 guard words changed every trial,
  520,000-556,000 NaN outputs per trial.
- `--block-size 256`, same workspace allocation: clean on 10/10 trials across
  both runs — 0 guard words changed, 0 NaNs, exact output.

The mechanism reproduces consistently across both architectures: the same
workspace allocation (196608 bytes) is safe at block_size=256 and unsafe at
block_size=128, on both a datacenter H100 and a consumer laptop GPU.

This confirms the underlying failure mode is real: an Inductor split-scan
kernel launched with a block size below the workspace's sizing minimum
silently writes past its allocated workspace, corrupting adjacent memory,
rather than raising an error.

What I have not independently verified: whether Inductor's real
coordinate-descent tuner and autotune cache actually select and persist an
unsafe R0_BLOCK=128 config in practice, as opposed to this being demonstrated
via a hand-written kernel that mimics Inductor's split-scan codegen. I
recorded a `.best_config` file (attached, `evidence/unsafe-scan.best_config`)
showing `R0_BLOCK: 128, found_by_coordesc: true` around when I first hit the
nondeterminism on the H100, but I have not been able to re-locate a matching
entry in my current autotune cache to re-confirm it, so I'm including it as
originally recorded rather than freshly verified.

I also applied a patch inferred from the diagnostic
as a fix, and after doing so the crash/corruption
stopped occurring. I'm not attaching that patch or including its contents as 
I don't want to take responsibility for its correctness, since I haven't
reviewed the tuner/cache internals closely enough to vouch for it as a
general fix. Noting the outcome here in case it's a useful signal, not as a
verified solution.

I don't understand the tuner/cache internals well enough to propose a fix
myself, so beyond the note above I'm reporting the reproducible
memory-corruption mechanism in case it's useful to someone more familiar
with that code.

Ablation:
- backend=inductor, mode="max-autotune", dynamic=False: reproduces (standalone
  kernel; mirrors the split-scan codegen pattern)
- eager mode: not applicable (no compiled scan kernel exists)
